questions.question_text: Use a multiplication fact to calculate $37\div5$.

options.why: Used six groups of five but did not form another complete group from the seven left over.
Used the next multiple forty even though it is greater than the dividend.
Used the divisor as the remainder instead of subtracting thirty-five from thirty-seven.

questions.question_text: Which consecutive multiples of $6$ show the quotient in $47\div6$?

options.why: Chose two multiples below forty-seven, so they do not enclose the dividend.
Chose two multiples above forty-seven, so they do not enclose the dividend.
Added six repeatedly but started from a number that is not a multiple of six.
Used eight as the quotient even though the given fact has seven groups of eight.
Subtracted fifty-eight instead of the known product fifty-six from sixty-one.
Reduced the quotient by one without changing the product used to find the remainder.
Copied the quotient into the remainder instead of subtracting seventy-two from seventy-four.
Used the divisor as the remainder, which would make one more complete group.
Subtracted the quotient sixty-eight rather than the product nine times eight.

questions.question_text: Which fact should replace $7\times9=63$ when solving $60\div7$?

options.why: Moved to an even larger multiple, which is still above the dividend sixty.
Changed the divisor from seven to six instead of reducing the number of groups.
Stepped down by two groups, missing the closer usable multiple fifty-six.
Used eleven groups even though ninety-nine is greater than the dividend.
Used the product for ten groups but recorded nine as the quotient.
Used the divisor as the remainder rather than subtracting ninety from ninety-seven.
